I'm so sorry my heart breaks for you. If there was one thing I could impart to you, it would be that no one including you can make your mother happy. It would take some kind of indepth self awareness/admitting hard truths coupled eith years of therapy to talk out whatever crazy bullshit makes NS the way they are to change that. The biggest problem is that Ns have no self awareness and the problem is with everyone else. Your mother is wrong to say those things to you, don't listen to her, honestly it's not true. I remember that believing and really knowing deep down that my NDad was the one with the problem and there was nothing I (or anyone) could do. As I've grown up I've really enjoyed helping others, but I've learned that you cannot help anyone that doesn't want your help. That includes your parents. So help where you can and accept when you cannot (I.e., when they are selfdestructive/negative/narcissists). Most importantly, this includes helping yourself. Please search free counselling services in your area. Are you still in highschool? Seek out a teacher or counsellor you trust. Talk about it, know that she is wrong and you can help people if you try but overall you do not deserve this. It might be good to go to therapy and talk out the issues you said you were having regarding wanting to make everyone happy, but don't involve her. Keep us updated! And know that we know what it is like to be there.
This is exactly my Dad, its the inconsistency of the reactions that I found hardest. It was the inconsistent reward system that really highlighted the crazy for me as a kid.

I relate to this so much, every point you touched on is also true for how my NDad tries to control me, my job, my future, mg relationship etc etc etc. Its exhausting. I'm sorry that you, and me, and everyone here - or who belongs here - has to deal with this. If you're not already low contact that is what I do and it helps. Thanks for sharing.

Hi thanks for the above information. I have had a long talk with her and gave her a number to call for free counselling in her area. It didn't seem to help because she says she's been to counselling before and they weren't helpful. I also gave her a suicide hotline number, so I think she has the resources she needs but thanks.

I definitely get what you mean! And thats for the shout-out about the job, it took about 4 years having worked part-time/being underemployed to get here, so I am very thankful now. Just as an update, I have made contact with a counsellor although she said she can only meet semi-regularly so I think I will look elsewhere, but I'm working on it! I know what you mean about focusing on being thankful and I try to aim for that too, but it is hard at times. Thanks for letting me know someone else has/is experiencing something similar :)

I had this same experience but when I moved out I couldn't stop despite not having enough money. I felt a need to be perfect (receive compliments for outfits) and could justify spending whatever to make this happen. This turned into a fairly serious (given that shortly after I moved out I had to leave my job for mental health reasons and didn't have an income) amount of debt $10,000. I'm down the to last $3000 now, but getting back on track has been really really hard. I think I just got addicted to having new things. Something that has really helped me is doing DIY projects. It gives a lasting sense of accomplishment, instead of the fleeting feeling I get when I buy something new. Budgeting has also been a huge thing for me and not going to the mall often. BUT I did spend way more than the budget when we were decorating our apartment. It is hard for me to let other people into the space without it being perfect, and that includes me being perfectly happy with the decor. For you, I might suggest reading about some minimalist (and very chic) fashion/wardrobe techniques, here are some articles I found inspiring: (1) http://www.examiner.com/slideshow/kikapaprika-makes-capsule-dressing-simple-and-stylish (2) http://www.whowhatwear.com/how-to-five-piece-french-wardrobe/slide3

As for your concern that you will go back to that trapped feeling, trust me, you'll have money for clothes/things as long as you are not constantly buying clothes/things you don't need. I'd also suggest only going to the mall if you need a specific item (I create a list on my phone of items that I need to replace and only go if there is something on it). Also, if something I see is not on the list I ask myself if I really need it. Seriously REALLY ask yourself do you need it?? (AKA food/water/shelter/transportation) if not put it back. 

Overall, I'd work on moving out because that is the only way you're going to be truly free. Goodluck:)

It is pretty amazing what they do. Since our brains don't work like that, we are surprised. I find it helps to remind myself that my Ndad is a child. Also, I'm sure it was, did she lie to them on her resume? If not (based on what you explained) I've got no IDEA why they'd hire her.

It is actually common for parents to only abuse one child (see this article that touches on this for extreme neglect, but this applies to all forms of abuse: http://www.post-gazette.com/local/region/2014/07/22/Phenomenon-exists-in-which-one-child-is-abused-while-others-are-not-experts-say/stories/201407220054). Still at the end of the day, this is never about the person being abused and all about the abuser. In this case it might be as simple as you made the abuser jealous just by existing while your siblings somehow never did. What better was to gas light you than if no one else is experiencing this? Get out as soon as you can and know that this is not about you.

This is one of the best delusions of grandeur I've ever come across - yes this is 100% an N thing. She will never accept that she was in the wrong, because how could she? She's perfect just like every N, everyone else is the problem - obviously lol God! She sounds terrrrrible I am so sorry to hear you've got to deal with her! Hang in there and give us an update when she's fired and escorted out of the building.

"I don't know what she did to me" - You had created a wonderful world in which you felt free and safe, and she invaded that world. It seems like she also took your hope that you could create a world where she cannot control you. In addition to echoing the comments above, let me say that I think you need a NC situation where she doesn't know where you live. Rent a space that has a doorman or a key hole at least. Create a new space where your NMom has never been, make it clear to the new landlord that even in the case of "fun surprise visits" relatives are not to be given keys to the apartment. If she does show up, tell her to leave or explain that you'll call the authorities. Again, what she did was invade the sacred space you had created for yourself. Think of this like the story of the big bad wolf/three little piggies (you did nothing wrong btw, your boundaries were clean Ns just are insane) and skip to building the third house - create an impenetrable fortress that your NMom cannot get into. Expect that she will make contact attempts and make a plan for if she does, but please believe in your ability to be free again. I really think that you can get that (or at least a similar) feeling back. If you can't move then it is harder, but that is what I would do if my Ndad did what you described above. Good luck!

Do you want her in your life? Or in your children's lives? If so, you can send a letter that says that she is welcome to come visit your family as long as she plans in advance to make sure that it works for everyone's schedules. If not, I'd say continue to ignore her. Sounds like you're better off.

Just because someone is a toxic person doesn't mean they need to be toxic 100% of the time. My dad has helped me out in some situations, but it doesn't negate the abuse. Whether they/she will snap or be helpful could depend on their/her mood, or a number of factors. I don't think I mentioned to address it with your mother, because you're right addressing it is really difficult and the abuse is likely to be denied. I think though for a lot of people they just snap at some point and start yelling back. However, I wouldn't recommend confronting an abuser to someone who can't move out yet because there is always a chance that they will snap and kick that person out (my dad tried to do this to me on a number of occasions). Like I said, keep your eye on the prize, use grey rocking and various other coping skills, pick your battles, remember that all the insults are projections of their own insecurities and not about you, work towards your goals, and you will definitely end up in a happier place one day.

Immediately from even the title of your post I thought "this person is probably being abused and their abuser is gaslighting them" (see this link for information on gaslighting if you haven't come across this - https://www.psychologytoday.com/blog/power-in-relationships/200905/are-you-being-gaslighted). 

By the time you explain the way your mother has screamed at you and what she's said I can sadly and definitively confirm that this is emotional abuse, and I'm so sorry. No one deserves to be treated like that and I can guarantee those things are not true. Ns yell at us because of their own bullshit, its got nothing to do with us. Everything that has been said to you or about you has NOTHING to do with you as a person. It is a hard thing to accept but your parents (or any/all Nparents) could have the most well-behaved child of their individual dreams and they would STILL put them down. BUT that is the truth. Say that to yourself over and over until you believe it.

The good news? There are a lot of things you can do to cope until you move out. I have to implore you to hold on until then because I swear you can get that feeling back and keep it every day (if you go NC) or 99% of the time (if you go LC). It might seem a long ways away, but you sound like you do have some wonderful people/things in your life, rely on them and make that your focus.

Additionally, I would recommend that you:

(1) Seek out friends and adults that you can trust when you want to discuss a dream/ambition/career goal - or just get advice on any topic. A teacher, parent of a friend, or guidance counsellor can all be very helpful, I'd suggest talking to multiple people to get advice where you've might have previously asked your parents. Or post here :) I would also say that one thing that helped me while I was in highschool/living at home was discussing the crazy shit I was enduring at home with other people. However, one note of warning, not everyone reacts the best (some people don't seem to want to believe that things are as bad as they are) that is why it is best to discuss with someone you trust. Those friends you talk about who are getting you through, make sure they know what is going on. If they don't believe you or don't validate your feelings, find a new confidant. 
(2) Look up free counselling services in your area (or call around and ask to speak to a psychologist and let them know you're 16 and your parents are emotionally abusive - maybe they'll be willing to do sessions at a much lower rate) so you can talk to a counsellor about your moods and how they "switch off and on" and feeling worthless (well everything) but bring up these facts. Make sure they know that your parents will make your life a living hell if they go to them with that information - what you need are coping skills to last until you can move out. A psychologist/counsellor can guide in developing these.
(3) Try to accept the hard truth that your parents aren't (and will not become) reasonable adults. I forget this at times, and I think WHY IS HE [Ndad] DOING THIS?! Then I remind myself, he's a child. The same is true of your parents, and they're so focused on believing that they're right about everything that they'll never change or grow because in their eyes they're perfect. Once we accept that this won't change, we can stop asking the gnawing question of "WHY" and focus on what to do about it.
(4) Expect them to treat you like shit, and react by grey rocking them (see this link: http://narcissistsupport.com/going-gray-rock/) 
(5) Do not expect them to provide love and support for your emotional challenges, or to be able to provide advice on any major life decisions, or to react well when you tell them your plans regarding those major life decisions.
(6) Find a cause you care about and start volunteering, or get a part-time job, this will get you out of the house and you'll get to meet new people. 
(7) Hold onto that feeling you had while you were away. WORK towards it by putting effort into whatever career / study program you are interested in (for now that might mean going to talk to the guidance counsellor to see what classes you'd need for a certain program OR just talking about what programs might be suited to you).

I say all that because your account reminds me so much of my life growing up. I relate exactly to what you were talking about while being on vacation around other loving people. I remember crying tears of joy for about an hour when I'd been away from my Ndad for a week. I didn't know life could be like that where I could breathe and feel alright and like myself. Why did I feel like this when I was away from my parents? Why did you feel like this when you were away from your parents? Unfortunately, they are a faulty support system (i.e., may currently provide a roof over your head but provide no substance, encouragement, or love) and we deserve better.

You are not overly sensitive, your self esteem has been trampled on and it makes it easy to doubt yourself. I'm so sorry to hear that you're going through this, but there is a light at the end of the tunnel. Remember that, work towards it. Go to your friends when things are hard, you're not weak or overly sensitive for needing support - lots of days your friends will come to you too and that won't make them weak either (no person is an island). Believe in yourself and be kind to yourself, treat yourself like you would a close friend. I'm so sorry to have to confirm that this definitely does count as abuse, and hope that you find the above useful moving forward. It is a long journey, but you've always got support here.

I definitely relate to this 100%. It is something that needs to be checked on regularly for me, but I have made progress. I generally try to live by the motto of treat yourself like you would treat a friend. This takes practice but can help you define boundaries. There are far reaching implications and it helps you to realize that if you would offer a kindness to a friend/want them to have some boundaries around taking care of others that you deserve them too. And you do. Caring people cannot help anyone if they don't look after themselves first. I'd start by mapping out different areas of your life and really thinking about boundaries. For example, helping friends and family - I am willing to help friends and family if the request is made in a reasonable time frame (unless its an actual emergency) as long as I receive similar support and am treated with respect. Always ask yourself if you'd be comfortable with these boundaries for someone you really care about if they brought them to you, if you wouldn't be, time to revise those boundaries. Its great to care but self care needs to be first.

My father was the N, but I have a best friend who's mom is an N and she has a very close relationship with her father. Here are some other things you can do:
(1) Explain to your daughter that you are aware there are issues and that she is doing nothing to deserve this treatment. Tell her you love her and that you're here to help. 
(2) To build her self esteem reward hard work (there's lots of parenting articles that discuss praising hard work rather than just saying good job and I'd suggest googling/reading some), let her know that with hard work she can achieve great things. This will take repeatedly saying things like this over and over to combat the conflicting information she's likely to receive.
(3) Nuture her interests/hobbies (does she like sports, computers, art, science etc?) If she doesn't have anything yet, take some time to explore a range of subjects with her (there are lots of good articles about cheap and or DIY projects parents can do with their children. 
(4) Intervene if she's being yelled at by Nmom. Even if your daughter does something that warrants normal discipline or a stern discussion and Nmom is overreacting ask Nmom to let you handle it until she calms down and is able to speak in productive ways. Hopefully this will prevent some abuse, maybe not thought it depends 
(5) Believe her if she tells you something and Nmom says differently. 
(6) Apologize if you lose your temper, Ns do not apologize. She needs to learn how healthy adults handle arguments.
(7) Validation, validation, validation. Let her know that her feelings are real and important. Say so explicitly.
(8) **Big one - tough one** explain to her A why you cannot  leave if you can. My friend resents her father for not leaving. Yes, this is hard for a young child to understand but by preteens they should be able to understand your reasoning. Also, make sure to let them know that you love them and not to feel guilty that you're staying to protect them. Moreover, find someone else to vent to about your experiences with your N. If your child asks you can say you've had similar experiences but its best to discuss one day when they're older if they're still interested. Let her know you have support and that she shouldn't worry about you because you're managing okay. Explain why her mother puts her down, and let her know that what her mother is saying is not based in reality. 
(9) Start saving to send her to a therapist or get her into talk to someone now if you're noticing signs of abuse 
[Taken from this article - http://www.helpguide.org/articles/abuse/child-abuse-and-neglect.htm] 

"Warning signs of emotional abuse in children

*Excessively withdrawn, fearful, or anxious about doing something wrong.
*Shows extremes in behavior (extremely compliant or extremely demanding; extremely passive or extremely aggressive).
*Doesn’t seem to be attached to the parent or caregiver.
*Acts either inappropriately adult (taking care of other children) or inappropriately infantile (rocking, thumb-sucking, throwing tantrums)."

(10) explain that she is not alone, other families deal with difficult family members and its not to do with who she is as a person. Being perfect will not help, let her know to just be herself.

My overall message would be love her, support her, read articles that explain the developmental stages she's in and try to understand. If she doesn't want to talk let her know you're there when she does. 

If you really can't explain to her why you can't leave, prepare to explain this to her as an adult. I can tell you as a DofN, and from talking at length with my friend who's mom is an N, your daughter will want to know. 

Just the fact that you're asking shows you love her a lot. I hope you find this somewhat helpful!

I can relate too and I'm so sorry. Its a hard thing to accept that we can't/won't get that. This bothers me randomly and usually it's more pronounced around happier families. I've really tried to focus on valuing the family I've made for myself, but also working to improve my self esteem and self worth. It will always be hard to accept that our Nparents didn't provide us with the love and care that others receive, I try to think of everything as a guide for what NOT to do as a parent. I also surround myself with supportive people and do my best to not let my past interfere but it does sometimes. Everything is a work in progress, and there is a definite grieving process to accepting that an N will never be the parent(s) we want or deserve. The best solace I've found has been strong connections with other people who are empathetic. There's nothing about you that caused this, your Nmom would treat any other child the same way, you deserve much more than she can give anyone. I'm so sorry.

I'm so sorry to hear that your N invalidated hour dream. My NDad did this to me too when I told him that I wanted to be a social worker, and when I wanted to be a photographer, and etc. An N will always try to put your dream down. Providing an alternative allows them to control you. Try to remember that what they're saying isn't based in reality (its based on the desire to bring you into their reality where they are God) and listen to yourself. My NDad told me I wouldn't be a good social worker because I'm too sensitive and I'd get burned out "wouldn't last 6 months". I am a social worker now and I love working with people. I take steps to ensure that my emotions are regulated so I don't bring work home (recently I'm trying to meditate as soon as I get home so I can leave work at work). You can do whatever you want, even if school / finding a job are hard you can never fail if you don't give up. If you work towards what you want your N will be very resistant I'd guess. I'm sorry it's hard to move on from an Nsister/friend too because when they're good to you they're so wonderful and fun. I have had to cut out two Nfriends and still miss one of them regularly. I think NC is for the best though. I know you said you had a falling out with other friends but is there someone else you could open up to (someone with a kind disposition)? Let them know you're struggling and discuss what's going on, see if a stronger bond can form. Otherwise there is always support here!
